item.title: Who gets to be Italian? The rise and rise of Islamophobia in Italy
item.description:
Who gets to be Italian? The rise and rise of Islamophobia in Italy

Submitted by Dalia Ismail on Fri, 09/25/2026 - 13:30
Giorgia Meloni's announcement of a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools comes as the Italian right competes over the demonisation of Muslims
A Muslim takes part in a mass in Santa Maria in Trastevere church in Rome on 31 July 2016 (AFP)
Off

When Giorgia Meloni addressed hundreds of young supporters of her Brothers of Italy party in Rome on Sunday, she chose the school as a way of illustrating who she thought was and was not Italian. 

“It cannot be that, in an Italian classroom, Italian children are the ones who feel cornered because they have become the minority. It cannot happen,” the prime minister told Fenix, the annual festival organised by National Youth, Brothers of Italy’s youth wing. 

On Wednesday, Meloni’s government approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools and announced that a 30 percent cap will be imposed on children without Italian citizenship or poor knowledge of the Italian language in the first year of primary, middle and high school. 

Meloni described the measures as “common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate”.

The announcement comes as Italy moves towards an expected national election in 2027, with immigration, Islam and national identity once again central battlegrounds on the political right.

Meloni’s speech and the legislation immediately raised practical questions: who exactly is “foreign” and who is Italian? 

Italy already has guidelines recommending a 30 percent ceiling for pupils without Italian citizenship. The distinction between “Italian” and “foreign” children also rests on citizenship, rather than on where children were born or have grown up. 

Italy's citizenship system is based primarily on descent: children born in the country to non-Italian parents generally do not acquire Italian citizenship automatically. 

As a result, children who were born in Italy and have spent their lives there can still be officially classified as foreign citizens. And Meloni's intervention did not come in isolation.

A mosque in Mestre

Last week, a banner declaring “Your integration is our ruin” appeared outside a school in Mestre, on the mainland opposite Venice, in an area with a large Bangladeshi community. Nearby, at a public park used by Muslims for Friday prayers, “No Islam” and Christian crosses were painted on the ground and on a wooden structure.

The incidents come as a dispute over plans by members of Mestre's Bangladeshi community to build a permanent mosque and Islamic centre on the site of a former sawmill becomes increasingly heated. The community has bought the land, but the project requires approval from local authorities.

'We cannot allow an immigrant to become an Italian citizen so easily because then this citizen votes'

- Roberto Vannacci, Futuro Nazionale

One of the project's most vocal opponents has been Anna Maria Cisint, a European parliament member for the right-wing Lega party who has repeatedly campaigned against the construction of new mosques. 

In February, during a Lega protest outside the proposed site in Mestre, Cisint declared that the mosque would not be built if her political camp remained in power.

On the same Sunday that Meloni announced her school measures, Cisint appeared at the Lega’s annual rally in Pontida, the northern Italian town that has hosted the party's symbolic gathering for decades. 

She was joined on stage by four activists from Nemesis, a French far-right group that describes itself as feminist. The activists were wearing full-face veils. As people on stage and in the crowd chanted “take it off”, the women removed them.

“The threat is radical Islam,” Cisint told the rally. “We will never allow them to Islamise our home. Never.”

The convergence was striking. In Rome, Meloni warned that Italian children could become a minority in classrooms; at Pontida, a coalition politician warned of the country’s “Islamisation”; and in Mestre, a mosque dispute was enflamed by anti-Muslim slogans.

The rogue general

At the same time, another political force is trying to carve out space further to the right.

Roberto Vannacci, a former army general who first became a national figure after publishing a book attacking immigration, feminism and LGBTQ+ rights, entered the European Parliament in 2024 with the Lega. 

The “rogue general” later broke with the party and founded Futuro Nazionale, a new far-right movement that has made “remigration” - the removal of migrants from Italy - one of its defining themes. 

The party is now registering around eight percent in some opinion polls ahead of the next general election, while the Lega, still led by Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, has fallen below six percent. The figures have intensified a struggle over voters on the Italian right and over how far its politics on immigration and national identity can move.

It was against this backdrop that Vannacci made one of his most explicit statements yet about who should be allowed to become Italian. Speaking at a conference on urban security organised by a police union in Turin on 18 September, he argued that Italy should not make citizenship easier for immigrants.

“We cannot allow an immigrant to become an Italian citizen so easily because then this citizen votes,” Vannacci said. “And when he votes, he does not vote for the good of Italian citizens but for his own good.”

When challenged over whether he was simply worried that naturalised citizens would not vote for him, Vannacci replied: “I'm not afraid that they won't vote for me. I'm afraid that they won't vote for Italy.”

Who gets to be Italian?

The former general’s argument raises a fundamental question: what happens when the person born or raised in Italy actually becomes Italian. 

Fioralba Duma, an Italian-Albanian activist with the campaign group Italians Without Citizenship, told Middle East Eye that Meloni's remarks were particularly troubling because many of the children described as “foreign” have never known another country.

“It is sad, because you realise how little responsibility those in power take when dealing with such important issues, and how little they do to protect children and guarantee them equal opportunities,” she said.

'Petrol is approaching three euros a litre, and she is talking about girls wearing the niqab at school when there are no girls wearing the niqab at school'

- Ahmed Vall, Islamic Community of Rome

“Our struggle started 10 years ago - and for many people even earlier - but instead of reducing the number of people who are foreigners only on paper, that number continues to grow every year. We used to talk about newly arrived migrants. Today we are talking about third generations: the grandchildren of immigrants, born in Italy.”

Duma’s comments point to a contradiction that has become increasingly visible in Italy's political debate. 

Politicians can speak of “foreign pupils” in classrooms even when those pupils were born in Italy, have spent their lives in the Italian education system and may speak Italian as their first language.

Italy's citizenship law remains largely based on jus sanguinis, or citizenship by descent. A referendum in June 2025 sought to reduce from 10 to five years the period of legal residence required for non-EU adults to apply for citizenship. 

Around two-thirds of those who voted backed the proposal, but turnout was only around 30 percent, well below the 50 percent required for the result to be valid.

The Muslim threat narrative 

The controversy over the proposed mosque in Mestre shows how these arguments are playing out beyond the classroom.

Part of the city's large Bangladeshi community wants to turn the site of the former sawmill into a permanent Islamic centre capable of hosting up to 1,500 worshippers. But the project requires a change in the area's planning designation, and Venice's centre-right mayor, Simone Venturini, has opposed the project.

Muslim organisations, meanwhile, accuse politicians of turning Islam into a political threat by focusing on issues that have little bearing on the everyday reality of Muslims in Italy.

Ahmed Vall, president of the Islamic Community of Rome, described Meloni's announcement on the niqab as “propaganda”. “We have never seen girls going to school wearing the niqab. It is a false problem,” he told MEE.

“Petrol is approaching three euros a litre, and she is talking about girls wearing the niqab at school when there are no girls wearing the niqab at school,” he said.

Vall said his organisation was prepared to challenge discriminatory measures through legal means, pointing to a complaint already filed against Lega MEP Silvia Sardone after she filmed and confronted a woman wearing a niqab in Turin. 

Rula Mohamed, another Islamic Community of Rome activist, described the situation more starkly, telling MEE that Islamophobia in Italy had reached “extreme levels”.

“What we are seeing today is the extreme result of something that has been cultivated for years,” she said. This climate, Mohamed argued, had been built not just by the right wing, but through years of Muslims being portrayed in the media as dangerous and incompatible with Italian society.

This, she said, had been compounded by the failure of much of the centre-left to seriously confront Islamophobia.

item.title: Pakistan look forward to ‘big test’ as Thailand loom in FIFA Asean Cup opener
item.description:
Pakistan will begin their campaign in the inaugural FIFA ASEAN Cup against a vastly higher-ranked Thailand on Saturday, with head coach Nolberto Solano describing the tournament as an opportunity for his side to measure themselves against some of Asia’s stronger teams.

The Group B Division One opener will kick off at 4:00pm local time (2:00pm PST) at the Si Jalak Harupat Stadium, with Pakistan then scheduled to face the Philippines on Sept 29 and Vietnam on Oct 2.

“We want to use this opportunity to test ourselves against teams like Thailand, Philippines and Vietnam,” Solano said at the pre-match press conference on Friday. “It’s an honour to be here and we know it will be a tough competition.”

The challenge facing Pakistan is reflected in the FIFA rankings. Thailand are currently 94th, while Pakistan are 198th in the latest official rankings.

The Philippines are 135th and Vietnam 113th.

“All our opponents will be very tough and they have fantastic players,” Solano said. “Asian football has been getting better and better so it is a big test for us.

“We are slowly growing, we try to go step by step. We will try to prove ourselves as a national team and see how far we can go in this competition.”

For Pakistan, the tournament comes after an encouraging summer in which Solano’s side won the Diamond Jubilee International Football Tournament in the Maldives.

Pakistan went unbeaten in the four-team event, drawing 0-0 with Bangladesh before beating the Maldives 3-0 and Afghanistan 2-0 in the round-robin stage. They defeated Afghanistan by the same score in the final, with Shayek Dost and Harun Hamid scoring, to secure their first standalone international tournament title in decades.

The triumph also ended a long wait for Pakistan to reach and win a standalone tournament. Their previous final appearance had come at the 1962 Merdeka Cup, while their last tournament triumph before the Maldives success had been a shared title at the Asian Quadrangular Football Tournament in 1952.

The ASEAN Cup, however, presents a markedly different proposition.

Thailand have named a squad featuring veteran playmaker Chanathip Songkrasin, Japan-based midfielder Supachok Sarachat and English-born forward Jude Soonsup-Bell. German-based defender Nicholas Mickelson is also in the squad, under English coach Anthony Hudson.

Thailand’s squad also includes established domestic names such as Supachai Chaided of Buriram United and Peeradon Chamratsamee of Port FC, underlining the depth available to the side.

Pakistan, meanwhile, have assembled a 23-man squad that combines domestic players with a number of footballers based abroad. Captain Abdullah Iqbal will lead the side, while experienced forward Kaleemullah has returned to the national setup.

Defender Easah Suliman, who plays abroad, joined the squad in Bandung after his arrival was delayed by illness. Twenty-two members of the squad had assembled in Indonesia by Thursday, with Easah expected to link up on Friday.

The Pakistan side also includes teenage midfielder Abdul Samad, captain of the national Under-17 team, who recently signed a two-year contract with Azerbaijani champions Qarabag.

For captain Abdullah, the tournament represents a chance for the players to test themselves against opposition of a different calibre.

“It is a great opportunity for us to compete against teams at another level,” he said. “We will try to give our best.”

The FIFA ASEAN Cup is the first edition of a new FIFA tournament involving 14 teams — all 11 ASEAN members plus Bangladesh, Pakistan and Hong Kong China as guest participants. Division One, being staged in Indonesia, comprises eight teams divided into two groups, with the group winners advancing to the final and the runners-up playing for third place.

Pakistan are in the same group as three teams with considerably stronger recent records in Asian football. After Thailand, they face the Philippines on Sept 29 before meeting Vietnam on Oct 2, with all three group matches being played in Bandung except Pakistan’s final fixture against Vietnam, which is scheduled for Jakarta.

For Solano, the immediate objective is less about the size of the challenge and more about how his players respond to it.

“We are slowly growing,” the former Peru international said. “We try to go step by step. We will try to prove ourselves as a national team and see how far we can go in this competition.”

item.title: PM Tarique puts ‘Bangladesh First’ vision before world
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has used his maiden address to the United Nations General Assembly to present a post-transition vision of Bangladesh built around political and economic empowerment, seeking international partnership to turn the country into a manufacturing hub while declaring: “Bangladesh First: Bangladesh for All.”
Addressing the 81st UN General Assembly in Bangla in New York on Thursday, Tarique laid out what he called a “3-R” strategy -- Recovery, Restoration and Reconstruction -- for rebuilding the country following the political upheaval of 2024.
The 21-minute address, delivered early Friday Bangladesh time, ranged from Bangladesh’s democratic transition and economic ambitions to the Rohingya crisis, climate change, Palestine, artificial intelligence, migration and global conflicts.
“A state cannot become strong while keeping its citizens disempowered,” Tarique said, pledging to build a prosperous, self-reliant and democratic welfare state where people could live with equal rights and dignity regardless of political affiliation, religion or ethnicity.
In one of the central economic messages of the speech, the prime minister said Bangladesh wanted to capitalise on its demographic dividend by transforming its working-age population into skilled human resources, creating large-scale employment and developing the country into a “manufacturing hub”.
He invited development partners to join that effort and said $50 million had been allocated in the current fiscal year to support start-ups led by young entrepreneurs, researchers and innovators.
Tarique also told the international community that Bangladesh welcomed partnerships, innovation and domestic and foreign investment as the government sought to create what he described as a safe, stable and business-friendly country.
On the Rohingya crisis, the prime minister delivered an unequivocal message: the crisis originated in Myanmar and its solution must also be found there.
“The only solution to this problem is the safe repatriation of the displaced Rohingya population to their homeland, Myanmar,” he said, noting that Bangladesh has sheltered more than 1.2 million Rohingyas for over nine years.
He called for firm international support for a lasting solution and urged continued life-saving assistance until repatriation, warning that failure to ensure justice for the displaced population could lead to another humanitarian crisis.
The prime minister also brought Bangladesh’s domestic political transition before the global forum. He described the previous 15 years as a period of “fascist rule and exploitation” and said Bangladesh was now returning to democracy following the 2024 mass uprising and the February 12 national election.
Those characterisations reflected the government’s political account of the transition presented in the speech.
Tarique said his government wanted not only electoral democracy but also the “democratisation of the economy”, so that economic growth reached every family and citizen.
He highlighted Family Cards, Farmers’ Cards, Sports Cards and e-Health Cards, and announced plans to consolidate different assistance programmes under a “Universal Card”.
The Family Card, issued in the name of the female head of a household, was presented as part of the government’s approach to women’s economic empowerment.
Education also featured prominently.
Tarique said the government planned to gradually raise education spending to 5% of GDP over five years, with greater emphasis on technical, practical and employment-oriented education.
On climate change, he sought stronger global action on climate justice, finance and adaptation, while highlighting plans to plant 250 million trees, excavate 20,000 kilometres of canals and advance the Teesta Master Plan and Padma Barrage project.
The prime minister also warned against a new global inequality emerging around artificial intelligence.
“We do not want the digital divide of today to evolve into an artificial intelligence divide in the future,” he said, calling for technology transfer, capacity building and affordable access to modern technology for developing countries.
He urged the UN to develop an effective framework to ensure AI and social media advances were used positively.
On international conflicts, Tarique said dialogue, diplomacy and cooperation should replace military solutions, while reiterating Bangladesh’s support for disarmament and an independent Palestinian state.
With Bangladesh approaching graduation from least-developed-country status, he also called for continued financing, greater market access, technology transfer and capacity-building support to make the transition sustainable.
Tarique closed by setting out the broader political message he wanted to attach to Bangladesh’s next phase: a country where young people could pursue their ambitions without fear, women could live with confidence and every child could have the opportunity to realise their potential.
“That is why we say, ‘Bangladesh First: Bangladesh for All’,” he said.

item.title: Bangladesh reaffirms support for independent, sovereign State of Palestine
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam has reiterated Bangladesh’s call for an independent, sovereign and viable State of Palestine on pre-1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital, and for Palestine’s full membership in the United Nations.
Shama Obaed attended the High-Level Ministerial Meeting of the Global Alliance for the Implementation of the Two State Solution, held at the UN Headquarters in New York on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly on September 24.
State Minister Shama Obaed called for accelerated implementation of UNSCR 2803 arrangements with clear accountability and Palestinian ownership, protection of UNRWA’s mandate and sustained funding, prevention of forced displacement and demographic change in Gaza and an end to settlement expansion.
The meeting was attended by Ministers and senior representatives from Member States and international organizations, who discussed concrete steps to advance the implementation of the two-state solution.

Cox’s Bazar airport new terminal set to open next week
item.description:
The newly built terminal at Cox’s Bazar airport will open for domestic passenger operations next week, ahead of planned international operations in October, marking a major step towards turning the tourism gateway into an international airport.
“From next week, the new terminal will be used for both arrivals and departures of domestic passengers,” Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) Chairman Air Vice Marshal Md Mostafa Mahmood Siddiq said.
The CAAB chairman, who made a final preparatory visit to Cox’s Bazar on Wednesday, said all domestic airlines operating at the airport had made the necessary preparations to shift their passenger-handling activities to the new terminal.
Airlines will initially use golf carts to transport passengers between aircraft and the terminal building, he added.
“After starting domestic operations, we will inaugurate international operations next month from this airport,” Siddiq said.
Director of Marketing and Sales at NOVOAIR Sohail Majid said the airline had completed all preparations and successfully conducted a test run to operate from the new terminal for its passengers.
“We have made all the necessary preparations, including deploying golf carts to use the new terminal,” he said.
The government is preparing to formally inaugurate Cox’s Bazar as an international airport in October following massive investment in upgrading the facility, including the construction of the new terminal and extension of the runway into the Bay of Bengal.
Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat earlier expressed optimism that Biman Bangladesh Airlines, as well as foreign carriers, would eventually operate international flights from the beach city.
CAAB Member (Operations and Planning) Air Commodore Abu Sayeed Mehboob Khan said, the terminal arrangement would switch to a hybrid system once international operations begin.
Under the planned arrangement, both arriving and departing international passengers will use the new terminal.
Domestic arriving passengers will then use the existing terminal, while departing domestic passengers will complete check-in formalities at the new terminal before proceeding to the old terminal to wait for boarding.
The new terminal forms part of a broader program being implemented by CAAB under the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism to upgrade Cox’s Bazar airport to international standards and make it capable of handling wide-body aircraft.
Currently one of Bangladesh’s busiest domestic airports, Cox’s Bazar handles an average of 28 to 30 passenger aircraft take-offs and landings daily.
CAAB has implemented two development projects and one technical project at the airport to expand its capacity and facilitate direct connectivity between the country’s premier tourism destination and international markets.
The international passenger terminal, covering around 17,956 square meters, has been constructed under a project with an approved cost of approximately Tk 362.63 crore.
The terminal includes a departure lounge capable of accommodating 450 international passengers, a duty-free shop, boarding bridge, lifts, escalators, conveyor belts, check-in desks, departure and arrival immigration counters and an arrival lounge.
Four immigration desks have been installed for departing passengers and six for arriving passengers, while two baggage delivery belts have been provided for international arrivals.
PA and Flight Information Display Systems (FIDS), signage, CCTV and heavy hand-luggage scanning facilities have also been incorporated into the terminal.
The airport’s annual passenger handling capacity is expected to rise from around 730,000 to 1.8 million following the expansion.
A 36,300-square-metre apron capable of accommodating two wide-body aircraft and three Dash-8 aircraft, along with two taxiways, has already been completed and incorporated into airport operations.
Parking facilities for 35 VIP and 90 general vehicles, internal roads and other supporting infrastructure are also included in the project.
The airport has also received ICAO certification following verification of the standards required for international operations.
Another major component of the transformation is the extension of the runway from 9,000 feet to 10,700 feet, making it the longest runway in Bangladesh.
Around 43 hectares of land have been reclaimed from the Bay of Bengal to extend the runway by 1,700 feet.
The extended runway is designed to accommodate fully loaded wide-body aircraft, including Boeing 777-300ER and Boeing 747-400 aircraft.
The runway extension project has an approved cost of Tk 3,709.61 crore, while the contract value is Tk 1,794.31 crore. Chinese joint venture CYWEB-CCECC JV has implemented the project.
The project also includes around 2,200 feet of precision approach lighting extending into the sea and installation of a CAT-II Airfield Ground Lighting system to facilitate safe aircraft operations.
A 1.89-kilometre protective embankment has been constructed to protect the runway from cyclones, storm surges and other natural disasters, while security fencing, patrol roads and an 8,149-metre drainage system are also part of the project.
The government expects direct international air connectivity to help attract more foreign tourists and stimulate investment in hotels, resorts and other tourism-related businesses in Cox’s Bazar.

Bangladesh, Trinidad and Tobago sign MoU on bilateral consultations
item.description:
Bangladesh and Trinidad and Tobago have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to establish regular bilateral consultations, with Bangladesh identifying energy cooperation as a priority for early discussions.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir and Trinidad and Tobago's Minister of Foreign and CARICOM Affairs SM Sobers signed the MoU in New York on Thursday, according to a press release received on Friday.
Kobir said the mechanism would allow the two countries to review their relations regularly, pursue commercial, economic, scientific, technical and cultural cooperation, and exchange views on regional and international issues.
He called energy one of the most promising areas for near-term cooperation and sought Sobers' support for an early technical meeting between relevant organizations from the two countries.
The Trinidad and Tobago participants could include the National Gas Company, Atlantic LNG, Phoenix Park Gas Processors and an ammonia or fertilizer producer, the release said.
Kobir also sought Trinidad and Tobago's support for sustained international attention to the Rohingya crisis, including during its 2027-2028 term on the UN Security Council. Bangladesh continues to shelter more than 1.2 million Rohingyas from Myanmar, he said, amid declining humanitarian funding.
He called for their safe, voluntary, dignified and sustainable return to Myanmar.
Describing cricket as a link between the two countries, Kobir proposed exchanges in youth and women's cricket, coaching, sports science and sports administration.
Both sides expressed hope that the MoU would make their longstanding friendly relationship more structured and substantive.

item.title: PM outlines 3-R strategy at UNGA to rebuild Bangladesh
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday told the international community that Bangladesh was pursuing a three-R strategy — Recovery, Restoration and Reconstruction — to rebuild the country after more than a decade-and-a-half of what he described as fascist rule and exploitation.
Addressing the general debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at UN Headquarters in New York, he also called for resolving global conflicts through dialogue and diplomacy, while urging stronger international action on the Rohingya crisis, climate change, disarmament, migration and equitable access to technology.
“Bangladesh became free from fascism in 2024, bringing an end to more than one and a half decades of fascist rule and exploitation. Having freed itself from the scourges of enforced disappearances and killings, abductions, corruption, looting and money laundering that had become the norm under fascist rule, Bangladesh is now once again embarking on the path of democracy,” Tarique said.
He said an immense horizon of possibilities was now open before Bangladesh and the government had begun implementing extensive programmes to transform the country’s working-age population into skilled human resources by taking advantage of the demographic dividend.
Tarique said Bangladesh also wanted to develop as a “manufacturing hub” and sought support from development partners in this endeavour.
The government, he said, had allocated US$50 million in the current fiscal year to create opportunities for young entrepreneurs, researchers and innovators to implement start-up initiatives.
“Detailed measures have been taken to create extensive employment opportunities and develop Bangladesh as a ‘manufacturing hub’,” he said, seeking support from Bangladesh’s development partners in this endeavour.
The Prime Minister said more than half of Bangladesh’s population were women. and women were therefore at the forefront of all government plans for the country’s socio-economic transformation.
The government was giving priority to women’s education, employment and entrepreneurship, he said, adding that opportunities for cash financing for women, particularly in the small and medium-sized industries sector, had been expanded to support the creation of women entrepreneurs.
Tarique also said opportunities for free education for women up to the undergraduate level had been made available.
He said the government wanted to ensure not only electoral democracy but also the ‘democratisation of the economy’ so that the benefits of economic growth and prosperity reached every family and citizen.
To achieve this, the government had introduced support programmes for economically disadvantaged people through various social protection schemes, including the Family Card, Farmers’ Card, Sports Card and e-Health Card, he said.
“The government considers the ‘Family Card’, issued in the name of the female head of each household, to be a symbol of women’s economic empowerment,” Tarique said.
He said the government also planned to introduce a ‘Universal Card’ by integrating the cards introduced to provide support in every sector.
This was Tarique Rahman’s maiden address to the UN General Assembly. He delivered the speech in Bangla, as announced earlier by his office.
Standing on the same platform where his father, Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman, and mother, former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia, had addressed the world, Tarique said he was speaking for the interests of Bangladesh and its people and with the hope of a peaceful world community.
Paying tribute to the martyrs of Bangladesh’s Liberation War, he also recalled those killed and injured during the July-August 2024 mass uprising early on in his speech.
He said after a prolonged period of fighting fascism, Bangladesh had entrusted the Bangladesh Nationalist Party with the responsibility of governing the country through the February 12 national election, describing the people as the source of all political power.
The Prime Minister said human-made conflicts had created unrest, displacement and humanitarian crises in many parts of the world, while wars and conflicts were putting severe pressure on the global economy, energy security and inflation.
“We believe that any conflict should be resolved through dialogue, diplomatic processes and mutual cooperation,” he said.
He said equality, fairness, protection of mutual interests, respect and dignity should form the basis of bilateral and multilateral relations among states.
Tarique also reaffirmed Bangladesh’s commitment to general and complete disarmament, prevention of the proliferation of nuclear weapons and arms control.
He said Bangladesh would continue to support UN initiatives aimed at promoting global peace and humanity.
On the issue of Palestine, which featured as one of the earliest items in his speech, the Prime Minister said Bangladesh remained unwavering in its support for the legitimate demands of the Palestinian people, including their right to self-determination and to establish an independent State of Palestine.
The Prime Minister said Bangladesh had been sheltering more than 1.2 million forcibly displaced Rohingyas from Myanmar for more than nine years, putting immense pressure on the country’s resources, environment, security and local communities.
He said the source of the Rohingya crisis lay in Myanmar and, therefore, its solution also lay there.
“The only solution to this problem is the safe return of the displaced Rohingya population to their homeland, Myanmar,” he said.
Tarique called for firm and effective support from the UN and the international community for a lasting solution to the crisis.
He also urged the continuation of life-saving humanitarian assistance for the Rohingyas until their repatriation, warning that failure to ensure justice for them could turn the situation into a humanitarian crisis in the near future.
Highlighting Bangladesh’s vulnerability to climate change despite its limited contribution to global carbon emissions, the Prime Minister called for stronger global action at COP31 on climate justice, climate finance and adaptation support.
He said Bangladesh had launched a programme to plant 250 million trees across the country over the next five years and was emphasising clean and solar energy.
The PM also announced a programme to excavate 20,000 kilometres of canals across the country to help protect Bangladesh from floods and droughts.
The government, he said, had also begun implementing the Teesta Master Plan and the Padma Barrage project to increase freshwater flow to the Sundarbans and conserve water through large reservoirs.
He said Bangladesh had reaffirmed its commitment to transboundary water cooperation by signing the 1992 Water Convention.
Tarique said science and technology would shape the future, with artificial intelligence, biotechnology and other scientific advances creating new opportunities.
But he warned against allowing today’s digital divide to become tomorrow’s “artificial intelligence divide.”
He called for technology transfer, skills development and affordable access to modern technologies for developing countries.
“No country should be left behind in this advancement of science,” he said, calling on the UN to adopt an effective policy framework to ensure the positive use of artificial intelligence and social media.
The Prime Minister said Bangladesh remained committed to ensuring regular, safe and orderly migration and called for stronger global cooperation to protect the rights, dignity and welfare of migrants.
As Bangladesh prepares to graduate from the UN’s Least Developed Countries category, he sought continued international support in financing, market access, technology transfer and capacity building to make the transition sustainable.
He also stressed the importance of trade facilitation, connectivity and regional cooperation, saying countries could help one another achieve prosperity through greater economic integration.
As he outlined his vision for Bangladesh, the Prime Minister said "a state can never become strong by keeping its citizens powerless."
He said Bangladesh wanted to establish a prosperous, self-reliant, welfare-oriented democratic state where people regardless of political affiliation, religion or race, could live safely with equal rights, respect and dignity.
“Bangladesh First: Bangladesh for All,” he said, outlining the government’s vision of a country where young people could pursue their dreams without fear, women could live with confidence and every child could realise their full potential.
The Prime Minister concluded by reaffirming Bangladesh’s unwavering support for the principles and values of the United Nations in the cause of world peace.
He addressed the 81st session of the UN General Assembly amid warm applause from delegates present at the UNGA Hall inside UN Headquarters in New York.
He took the podium at around 6:16pm local time to deliver Bangladesh’s national statement at the General Debate.
UNGA President and Bangladesh’s Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman presided over the session, as part of which he introduced the PM and invited him to address the assembly.
Wearing a black suit and red tie, Tarique walked up to the podium and began his address.
It was also a significant moment for the Prime Minister as his late father, President Ziaur Rahman, and mother, former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia, had previously addressed the UN General Assembly from the same podium.

item.title: Energy Department says nearly $2 billion will fund 26 U.S. locations to boost America’s aging power grid
item.description:
The Energy Department said Thursday that it will spend almost $2 billion to try to squeeze more electricity out of the nation’s aging and stressed power grid, as President Donald Trump’s administration steps up efforts to avoid blackouts amid skyrocketing energy demand spurred by artificial intelligence.

The money will go toward 31 projects across 26 states that are expected to produce more than 23 gigawatts of additional electricity capacity — enough to power 16 million homes. The projects will use new technologies such as sensors to measure real-time weather conditions to ensure safe transmission or direct power away from congested paths, the department said.

The upgrades could improve power reliability and lower electricity costs for about 100 million Americans, officials said.

“This is a quick way to lower electricity prices and increase reliability: using fibers that are already in the transmission lines to analyze what’s the temperature out, what’s the wind out, how can we use this transmission line to distribute more power, but safely and only in the right conditions,” Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a news conference promoting the grants Thursday at a PPL Corp. facility in Allentown.

The eastern Pennsylvania electric utility says two data centers in its territory came online this year and six more are under construction, with enough other data centers in the advanced planning stages that its peak electric demand could quintuple by 2032.

PPL said it is receiving $71.5 million to modernize an existing high-voltage transmission line across roughly 30 miles in northern Pennsylvania.

The announcement comes amid warnings that AI’s voracious demand for power is threatening to overwhelm U.S. power supplies, as massive new data centers come online faster than new power plants can be built. It also comes as electricity bills rise faster than inflation in many parts of the U.S., blamed in some areas on demand from data centers.

The snowballing opposition to data centers in communities across the country has thrown a wrench into the plans of the world’s richest companies and transformed the midterm election landscape.

Trump continues to stick up for data centers, even as politicians from both major political parties criticize them and many communities try to block them.

In the meantime, Congress and some states are trying to push utilities to expand their use of new technologies to make grids more efficient and to lessen the need to build new power plants.

Julia Selker, the executive director of the WATT Coalition, a trade association for grid-enhancing technologies, said both the projects and the scale of the investment are significant. Utilities in the U.S. are lagging places like Europe in adopting the technologies, despite federal investment in the past to develop and test them, Selker said.

Still, Drew Maloney, CEO of the Edison Electric Institute, a trade association of for-profit utilities, said America’s electric utilities are making a “significant investment” every year in new technologies to strengthen the grid and reduce outages.

Wright said that work on the projects should begin right away and that he hoped some efficiencies are in place before this winter to tamp down price spikes when extreme weather sends demand skyrocketing.

Wright said he didn’t know whether the projects would have gotten done without federal funding. Many, he said, had been under consideration before the grants were offered, but the grant recipients hadn’t “quite pulled the trigger” on them.

Projects being announced Thursday will involve component enhancements on more than 1,500 miles (2,400 kilometers) of transmission lines and technological enhancements across nearly 21,000 miles (34,000 kilometers), the department said.

Projects were prioritized based on those that can be put into operation quickly, officials said. Money for the grants comes from the bipartisan infrastructure law enacted by Congress under then-President Joe Biden, a Democrat. The government’s $1.9 billion in funding will be matched by $3.35 billion from the recipients, the department said.

Recipients include utilities, cooperatives and four state agencies. The state agencies — in Colorado, Indiana, Ohio and Oklahoma — were the biggest recipients, collectively drawing $810 million, with the Colorado and Oklahoma projects promising improvements to regional grids.

Trump has vowed to “unleash” the nation’s energy sector in his second term, aiming to drive up record-setting domestic oil and gas production, strip away pollution restrictions on power plants and keep expensive coal-fired power plants operating past their retirement dates.

The administration also has pledged nearly $4 billion to buy back offshore wind leases as Trump seeks to discourage the expansion of wind energy in favor of fossil fuels.

His administration meanwhile has pushed to help tech giants build and connect data centers to power plants and high-voltage power lines and convert Cold War-era uranium enrichment plants into data center and power plant complexes.

—Marc Levy and Matthew Daly, Associated Press

item.title: Polymarket faces a lawsuit in New York with claims it’s operating an illegal gambling platform
item.description:
New York sued the prediction market Polymarket on Thursday, arguing the platform is an unlicensed gambling operation and calling for a judge to block the company from operating in the state.

The lawsuit is the latest legal challenge from a state moving to rein in popular and now-ubiquitous betting apps that allow people to place wagers on most anything, including sports, weather, elections and technology.

Prediction market platforms have argued states do not have the authority to govern them because they are regulated at the federal level by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

New York officials filed Thursday’s lawsuit against Polymarket in state court and want the company to face fines and be forced to pay restitution to users because the platform did not get a gaming license from the state. The state has previously sued other platforms such as Kalshi, Coinbase and Gemini using a similar argument.

“By running an unlicensed gambling operation, Polymarket has done more than just knowingly violate state law, they have put New Yorkers at risk, especially those underage who are most vulnerable to problem gaming,” Gov. Kathy Hochul said in a statement.

In a statement, Polymarket’s Chief Legal Officer Neal Kumar said, “We’ll fight for our users.”

“Polymarket was founded in a tiny NYC apartment and now has more than 350 employees here, embodying why people and businesses come here to make it. We believe in New York and we’re staying here,” Kumar said.

Prediction market platforms have said they operate differently than traditional gambling operations, because consumers are trading against other consumers, similar to how stock markets work. They allow participants to buy and sell contracts tied to the probable outcome of an event. The platforms say prices are based on trading and they only take a fee from the trading.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which has opposed state regulation of the platforms, did not immediately return a request for comment.

—Associated Press

item.title: Iran’s Regime Is Weaker Than It Looks
item.description:
For five and a half years, I was a hostage of the Islamic Republic of Iran. During that time, I came to believe something about the regime that may seem improbable from the outside: It is far weaker than it looks. Today, I believe we are closer to its end than many Americans realize.

As America approaches the November midterm elections, calls to turn inward will inevitably rise. There will be arguments that we have done enough, that the Islamic Republic is someone else’s problem, that the costs are too high or the outcome too uncertain. Giving in to that temptation would be a historic mistake.

After 47 years, the regime that has inflicted unimaginable misery on its own people and helped spread militant extremism throughout the Middle East may be approaching its final act. This is not the moment to lose our resolve.

Long before Americans became familiar with terrorist organizations such as Hezbollah, Hamas, al-Qaeda, and ISIS, and long before the attacks of September 11, 2001, the Islamic Republic was using religious extremism, hostage-taking, and terrorism as instruments of statecraft. It directly nurtured organizations such as Hezbollah and Hamas and helped create a regional environment in which hatred of the West and political violence could flourish.

But the greatest victims of the Islamic Republic have always been the Iranian people themselves. The 1979 revolution was an Iranian one, and the country has lived with its consequences ever since. Nearly half a century later, a different generation is demanding the right to chart an alternative course.

During my years in captivity, I watched a nation seemingly trapped in a downward spiral of corruption, incompetence, and cultish ideological obsession. Every evening, my cellmates and I watched “Akhbare Bisto-See,” or “20:30 News,” on Iran’s state-controlled IRIB Channel Two—a nightly parade of propaganda, arrogance, ignorance, and hatred.

After my first few weeks in Section 2A of Evin Prison, controlled by the intelligence arm of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, I began conducting a private, admittedly unscientific experiment. I watched the news, observed what was happening around me, talked to as many inmates as I could, and estimated how many years it would take Iran to catch up with the modern world.

Fifty years, I thought. Then 75. Then 100. After eight months, when my estimate reached 150 years, bewilderment set in. So I stopped counting.

What haunted me was not merely the country's physical and moral decay, corruption, or the government's incompetence. It was what decades of humiliation and hopelessness had done to people. Sometimes the evidence sat only a yard from me.

Two of my cellmates were members of ISIS. Both were Iranian Kurds. I could not understand it. They were not Arabs from Syria or Iraq. They were Iranians. How could young Iranian men join an organization as murderous as ISIS? Sometimes late into the night, I listened to their stories. Gradually, I began to understand that before extremism had recruited them, humiliation had prepared them.

One of those young men was Ibrahim. He had just turned 18 when I met him in communal Room 2 of Section 2A. One night, he told me about his younger brother’s death. His family was so poor they could not afford a simple burial. They carried the boy’s body on their shoulders to the outskirts of their village, dug a hole, and buried him without ceremony or even a memorial stone. “Like a dog,” Ibrahim told me. I have never forgotten those words.

Years later, I encountered another Iranian Kurd whose story has stayed with me.

After I was sentenced to 10 years in prison for what the Islamic Republic called “cooperating with the hostile nation of America,” an old friend arranged for a man to help me cross the border to freedom. I will call him Jafari.

We embarked on a 15-hour journey toward the northwestern frontier, but our luck ran out about 20 miles from the Iraqi border, when we were arrested by a field unit of the Ministry of Intelligence. The following day, in the city of Sardasht, Jafari and I waited to appear before a local judge on charges of attempting to cross the border illegally. We sat there, exhausted, our hands cuffed together. Until then, I knew almost nothing about him except that he was 30 years old and a Kurd.

As we waited, I listened as he spoke to the guards. I learned that he had previously spent 10 years in prison for belonging to a Kurdish political organization. Then he described what had happened when he was first arrested.

According to Jafari, while he was kneeling on the floor with his hands cuffed behind his back, his prosecutor unzipped his pants and urinated into his mouth, telling him that he and his Kurdish people were scum.

Looking at him sideways, I could see his eyes welling with tears. These were not tears of fear or anger. They were the tears of a young man whose dignity had been crushed.

There are certain things human beings cannot be expected to endure indefinitely.

I think of Ibrahim and Jafari when I think of the Iranians who have taken to the streets against the Islamic Republic.

To outsiders, demonstrations in Iran are often described in political terms: reformists versus hard-liners, secularists versus Islamists, protesters versus the government. But beneath the politics lies something more elemental: the systematic, prolonged humiliation of a proud nation.

For decades, Iranians have watched a country blessed with extraordinary human talent, history, natural resources, and culture grow poorer and more isolated, while a corrupt, insular ruling establishment enriched itself and demanded blind obedience.

For Iran’s ethnic minorities, that humiliation has often been compounded by discrimination and violence. Kurds, Azeris, Arabs, Baluch, Turkmen, and Lors have all, in different ways, experienced life on the margins of the Islamic Republic.

As for Iranian women, they require almost no explanation. We need only remember the name Mahsa Amini. Volumes could be written about their strength, courage, and dignity—and about the wrath inflicted on them by a deeply misogynistic regime. Mahsa Amini’s death became a symbol because millions of Iranian women recognized in her story the state’s intrusion into the most intimate decisions of their lives, backed by violence.

Iran’s religious minorities have their own disheartening stories. Jews, Baha’is, Zoroastrians, and Christians have lived for decades under suspicion, restrictions, and persecution.

In the yard of Ward 8 at Evin Prison, I once sat with a Baha’i man I had befriended. It was around noon on October 14, 2022, one day before prisoners rioted and fire engulfed part of Evin. I remember the conversation so vividly not because of what happened the following day, but because of the story this gentle man told me.

Back in 1980, his father had been hanged in that same prison, perhaps only 100 yards from where we were sitting. As a young boy, he had accompanied his mother to collect his father’s body. He told me his father's only crime was being a Baha’i. Nearly half a century later, the son was sitting inside Evin as well, just yards from where he had lost his father.

That is the Islamic Republic’s legacy: a seemingly endless cycle of violence, poverty, and humiliation.

It has had 47 years to build a prosperous nation. Instead, it built prisons, missile cities, and an expansive nuclear program while much of its population struggled.

It had 47 years to harness the extraordinary abilities of the Iranian people. Instead, millions left the country, while some of its brightest young minds ended up in prison cells.

Among them were Ali Younesi and Amirhossein Moradi, two kind, polite, extraordinarily bright young men with whom I had the privilege of sharing a cell in Ward 4 of Evin Prison. Younesi was an internationally recognized astronomy prodigy; Moradi, a gifted physics student. Both were in their early 20s and studying at the prestigious Sharif University. Their stories are repeated across Iran, where the Islamic Republic has spent decades crushing the hopes of some of the country’s most gifted young people.

It had 47 years to earn legitimacy. Instead, it demanded blind submission.

And that distinction matters now because Iran and the Islamic Republic are not the same thing. The regime wants the world to believe that any attack on its power is an attack on Iran itself. It wants Americans to believe that the alternative to the Islamic Republic must be chaos, civil war, or another extremist regime.

I do not accept that premise.

The Iranian people I came to know—including those I encountered in circumstances I would never have chosen—were not yearning for more ideology. They were yearning for dignity, prosperity, basic human rights, and a return to being respected members of the world community. They wanted decent-paying jobs. They wanted opportunity. They wanted justice. They wanted their daughters to live without fear. They wanted the freedom to worship—or not worship—as they chose. They wanted to belong to their country without being humiliated for being Kurdish, Baha’i, Christian, Jewish, Baluch, or anything else.

Above all, they wanted a future. That is why this moment matters.

Earlier this year, Iranians once again demonstrated their resolve. Many initially took to the streets over painfully familiar grievances: inflation, electricity shortages, water scarcity, economic mismanagement, corruption, and the relentless erosion of their purchasing power.

They were met with lethal force. Thousands were reportedly killed in the crackdown and tens of thousands arrested. But casualty figures alone cannot convey the particular cruelty of repression in the Islamic Republic.

For years, Iranian families and human-rights organizations have reported a practice sometimes described as “bullet money” or a “bullet fee”: authorities demanding payment from families before releasing the bodies of relatives killed by the state, in some accounts ostensibly to cover the cost of the ammunition used to kill them.

Think about what that means. Your son goes into the street to protest the cost of food. Your daughter demands the freedom to live as she chooses. They do not come home.

Then you go to retrieve the body of the child you raised, and the state that killed your child demands payment for the bullets before returning the body to you.

Statistics describe Iran’s economic decline. Its currency has collapsed. Inflation has ravaged household incomes. Corruption remains endemic. Millions of talented Iranians have left the country. All of those facts matter, but none captures the nature of the Islamic Republic quite like a grieving parent being asked to pay for the bullet that killed a child. That is humiliation. That is indignity.

And after 47 years, something fundamental is happening inside Iran. The Islamic Republic has survived through fear. Regimes built on fear can seem permanent until suddenly they are not.

I saw fear inside the Islamic Republic. But I also saw something the regime should fear far more. I saw what happens when humiliation turns into anger, when anger becomes courage, and when people told for decades that they are powerless—or scum—begin to realize they vastly outnumber those who oppress them.

The pressure is no longer merely political. Iran is confronting one of the most severe economic crises in the Islamic Republic’s history. Inflation has soared, the rial has fallen sharply, and the regime is struggling to obtain the foreign currency it needs to finance imports and sustain the state. A U.S. naval blockade has sharply curtailed Iranian oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, while tighter financial sanctions are closing channels Tehran once used to evade economic pressure. The Islamic Republic has survived crises before. But rarely has it faced this combination of domestic anger, economic exhaustion, international isolation, and pressure on the sources of revenue that sustain the state.

America should not determine Iran’s future. The Iranian people must decide that themselves. Nor should Washington confuse supporting the Iranian people with choosing their next government. We have learned enough from history to know the dangers of that approach. But an equally dangerous mistake would be abandoning people when they are closer to changing their circumstances than outsiders might realize.

The United States and its allies should maintain pressure on the institutions that sustain repression while making it unmistakably clear that our quarrel is with the Islamic Republic, not with Iran or its people.

We should amplify Iranians’ voices rather than presume to speak for them. And we should resist the temptation—especially when domestic politics becomes consuming—to trade long-term resolve for short-term political convenience.

The final act of this 47-year tragedy may already be underway.

If the curtain is finally beginning to fall on the Islamic Republic, it will not be Americans who take the stage for the finale.

It will be the Iranian people. Our responsibility is simpler: Don't abandon them as they prepare to take the stage.

We may be closer than we think.

item.title: New energy and trade routes could bypass Hormuz and change the Middle East. But major challenges remain
item.description:
New energy and trade routes could bypass Hormuz and change the Middle East. But major challenges remain Expert comment thilton.drupal 25 September 2026

The Strait of Hormuz crisis is accelerating a wider reordering of the region, as Iraq, Syria and Lebanon plan new oil pipelines and transport corridors. But whether they can seize the opportunity to diversify will ultimately depend on wider reforms.

The war on Iran and the resulting disruption to the Strait of Hormuz has exposed the vulnerability of existing trade and energy routes and unsettled the old balance of power across the Middle East.

In this context, Iraq, Syria and Lebanon are seeking to capitalize on their position between Europe and the Gulf and improve their connectivity via oil and gas pipelines, roads, railways and digital corridors. Once central to an Iranian regional order, all three governments are now aiming to achieve greater sovereignty by diversifying their economic ties, a shift supported by the Trump administration. 

Yet they are attempting to do so while facing foreign occupations and military action, and while also confronting domestic endemic corruption and fragmented political systems that empower armed groups. 

Whether they can seize this opportunity to become more connected – and more sovereign – will therefore depend not only on the infrastructure they build, but on whether they can reform their states to govern it.

Changing energy routes

The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz has caused severe disruption to regional energy flows, including from Iraq. 

Pre-war, Iraq was exporting around 3.3 million b/d from its southern oilfields. By the second week of March, exports from southern Iraq had collapsed. Southern exports gradually recovered from mid-April, reaching 2.3 million b/d in August, aided by Iraq giving discounts for buyers and by Iran reportedly giving permission for Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the Strait.

Syria and Lebanon have been less directly impacted by Hormuz, given neither is a major oil exporter and they both have access to the Mediterranean. However, the crisis has spurred a potential wider reconfiguration of regional trade and energy routes, as countries like Iraq look for alternatives. 

Both Beirut and Damascus have an opportunity to position their Mediterranean ports and transport networks as gateways between the Gulf and European markets in a reconfigured regional trading system.

Iraq–Syria pipeline

Iraq is already pursuing several ways to diversify its export routes. Baghdad is seeking to expand exports through Turkey’s Mediterranean port of Ceyhan, where Iraqi crude already flows, and is even discussing the revival of a long-stalled idea for a pipeline to Jordan’s Red Sea port of Aqaba.

Iraq and Syria are also pursuing a new pipeline that would carry Iraqi crude oil westwards to the Mediterranean. This would aim to give Baghdad another alternative to its overwhelming dependence on exports through the Strait of Hormuz. 

This planned corridor is often described as a revival of the historic Kirkuk–Baniyas pipeline, which once carried oil from northern Iraq to the Syrian coast. But it entails new infrastructure to form a wider network connecting Iraq’s southern and northern fields to a hub at Haditha in western Iraq, from which oil could flow west through Syria to the Mediterranean port of Baniyas and north towards Turkey.

Estimates put the cost at around $15 billion, with construction likely to take around four years. The Trump administration is reportedly supporting the plan as part of a strategy to reduce Iran’s regional leverage by diversifying away from Hormuz. 

The new network, which has a proposed initial capacity of around two million b/d, would allow Iraq to divert a substantial share of its exports away from Hormuz, reducing Iranian leverage. But it would diversify rather than replace Hormuz: most Iraqi crude exports go to Asian markets, particularly China and India, which are far quicker to reach from the Gulf than the Mediterranean.

New East–West corridors 

Lebanon and Syria are also exploring the restoration of railway links that could eventually connect the Lebanese coast through Syria to Iraq, Turkey and the Gulf. This month, Lebanese and Syrian officials inspected a potential rail route connecting the Lebanese port of Tripoli to Homs in Syria. This could be the potential first step in re-establishing Syria as a transit state, with Tripoli as a potential Mediterranean gateway.

Yet while rebuilding the short Tripoli-Homs railway may seem feasible, establishing a wider regional corridor will require much more infrastructure and faces challenges. Lebanon’s previous plans to revive the same railway stalled before work began, in part over financing and mismanagement. Syria’s railway system is badly damaged by war, with the government estimating that its rehabilitation could cost around $5.5 billion. 

The same pursuit of connectivity is extending into the digital realm. New fibre-optic networks through Iraq and Syria are intended to give Gulf states alternative land routes for the vast quantities of data that currently travel through vulnerable submarine cables.

Energy under attack

For now, there is a considerable gap between ambition and reality. Iraq, Syria and Lebanon are pursuing these infrastructure projects in the shadow of a war they cannot control and while facing external occupations or interference. 

In Lebanon, Israeli forces occupy a self-declared security zone in the south, with more than a million people displaced. In Syria, Israel seized the demilitarized buffer zone in December 2024 and has maintained a military presence there since. 

Across the Middle East, energy infrastructure has become a major target, with over 100 attacks on energy assets in the first six months of the war. Iran has attacked energy facilities across the Gulf, while Israel has struck fuel storage depots and gas infrastructure within Iran. 

Iran retains influence through its political and armed networks across the region. This includes groups embedded within Iraq and Lebanon that have repeatedly demonstrated their capacity to threaten critical infrastructure. 

Related work

The Houthis’ capture of Mocha has transformed the war in Yemen – and the geopolitics of the Red Sea

In Iraq, for instance, the Khor Mor gas field has suffered repeated rocket and drone attacks blamed on militias. More recently, attacks launched from Iraqi territory forced the temporary closure of Saudi Arabia’s East–West pipeline, which is also designed to reduce Riyadh’s dependence on Hormuz. The Houthis have attacked Saudi oil tankers and seized the Bab al-Mandab Strait coastline this month.

The threat to infrastructure is not limited to Iran-aligned armed groups. Israel has repeatedly targeted transport infrastructure during the current conflict, including in Lebanon, demonstrating how the conflict can disrupt the physical networks on which greater connectivity would depend. And in eastern Syria, through which the proposed new Iraqi energy corridor would pass, armed groups including ISIS have attacked oil wells and tanker trucks.

Internal obstacles

Another obstacle is entrenched corruption. Iraq, Lebanon and Syria all sit near the bottom of Transparency International’s corruption perceptions index. 

In political systems where public contracting is a principal means of distributing rents, mega-projects can create opportunities for political parties to potentially profit from contracts, often at the expense of their delivery. 

Linked to this is the fragmentation of these states themselves. Infrastructure on this scale requires institutions capable of coordinating decisions over years, enforcing contracts, protecting assets and binding competing interests to a common project. 

Yet authority in Iraq, Syria and Lebanon remains fragmented among political factions, competing institutions and armed actors. This leaves governments unable to guarantee the security or financing of projects, with multiple actors able to obstruct their completion or extract rents. This creates a fundamental mismatch between the scale of ambition and the capacity to deliver it.

Connectivity doesn’t guarantee sovereignty 

The war has increased the strategic value of Iraq, Syria and Lebanon’s geographical position. As states and companies search for alternatives to Hormuz, the three countries offer potential alternative corridors connecting the Gulf to the Mediterranean and Europe.

Whether Iraq, Syria and Lebanon can take advantage of this opportunity will help determine whether they can shape the post-war regional order, or whether it is once again shaped around them. 

Want to hear more on the future of global trade?

Join us at our Global Trade Conference for expert analysis on the shifting rules of the global economy.

But connectivity is not the same as sovereignty. New pipelines, railways and trade corridors can offer these states alternatives to the dependencies of the old order, but alone they cannot produce sovereignty. That requires institutions capable of delivering and protecting these projects.

If Iraq, Syria and Lebanon want to seize the opportunities of the changing regional order, they will need to do more than build new routes across their borders. They will need to build states capable of governing these new connections, while ensuring that their benefits extend to their populations, not just elites.

item.title: The Guardian view on Trump and Xi: a show of friendship, but no real attempt to address the tensions | Editorial
item.description:
The Chinese leader’s visit to Washington appears to have done nothing to shift the stalemate in bilateral relations

Within days, two high-profile Chinese visitors will arrive in the US – envoys of friendship, as Xi Jinping described them when he met Donald Trump at the White House this week. The giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be hosted at Atlanta zoo. Beijing dispatched the first panda pair to the US in 1972 following President Richard Nixon’s landmark visit to China. It uses the animals to indicate satisfaction or displeasure with other nations. But it also charges heftily for their lease: reportedly, around $1m a year per pair. Americans’ views of China have warmed from a pandemic nadir, but are unlikely to be shifted much by two animals, however charming. These days they are more of a token gesture than a striking symbol.

It is telling that the announcement was one of the main takeaways of Mr Xi’s visit to Washington. Expectations were low after May’s stalemate summit in Beijing, but this meeting still struggled to meet them. The US president gave Mr Xi a lavish welcome – unusually, travelling to meet the “strong, vibrant and fit” Chinese leader off the plane. He insisted that they had “never gotten along better”.

The Takeaway: UN General Assembly debate Day 4
item.description: From the Caribbean to the Pacific, leaders from small island States demanded climate justice, ocean protection and greater solidarity at the UN General Assembly on Friday.  They warned that rising seas are already redrawing national boundaries, while the ripple effects of faraway wars are being felt on their shores. This edition of The Takeaway summarizes key points made during the fourth day of the annual high-level debate.

item.title: Saudi Arabia warns Gulf security inseparable from global stability amid regional tensions
item.description: Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Minister warned on Saturday that escalating threats across the Middle East risked international peace, energy security and global trade, calling for stronger international cooperation to protect Gulf States and vital shipping routes.

item.title: Cuba warns against ‘law of the jungle’ as Foreign Minister denounces US pressure
item.description: Cuba’s Foreign Minister warned the UN General Assembly on Saturday that escalating military and economic pressure in Latin America and the Caribbean was threatening international law, while accusing the United States of intensifying a decades-long campaign to isolate and weaken his country.

item.title: Lavrov issues call for new Eurasian ‘security architecture’
item.description: Russia's Foreign Minister, Sergey Lavrov, accused Western countries of destabilising the world through “force and double standards” in his address to the UN General Assembly on Saturday, vowing that Moscow's “special military operation” in Ukraine would be “carried through to the end.”

item.title: ‘Safeguard the postwar order,’ China tells UN General Assembly
item.description: China's Vice President, Han Zheng, urged the world to defend the postwar international order on Saturday, telling the UN General Assembly that geopolitical conflicts, widening development gaps and mounting global challenges make multilateralism more urgent than ever.

item.title: Countries far from conflict paying the price for wars not their own, India tells UN
item.description: India’s External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar warned on Saturday that violent conflicts continue to undermine international peace and security, while countries far removed from the battlefield are being forced to pay a heavy price.

item.title: Canada urges stronger partnerships as global order faces ‘rupture’
item.description: Canada’s Foreign Minister Anita Anand warned the UN General Assembly on Saturday that the international order has entered an era of profound disruption, calling for stronger multilateral cooperation and new partnerships as major powers increasingly turn away from global economic integration.

item.title: Five days inside the contradictions of the United Nations
item.description:
UNITED NATIONS: Only at the United Nations can a journalist walk through a corridor and suddenly find himself face to face with a prime minister, pause before a sculpture symbolising peace, read the words of a Persian poet written on a wall, and then rush outside to report on a protest against a war thousands of miles away.

For five days, I lived inside that extraordinary contradiction while covering the high-level debate of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York. The official high-level week brought heads of state and government from around the world to the UN headquarters between September 22 and 26.

The first thing one begins to notice at the United Nations is the art.

There are sculptures, statues and works donated by countries that seem to confront you at every turn. They are reminders of peace, humanity, war and the hope that nations can somehow learn to live together.

Even before you enter the United Nations, the place begins to tell its story.

As you approach the Secretariat Building, you encounter Barbara Hepworth’s Single Form, the large abstract bronze standing beside the circular pool. Donated by Jacob Blaustein, it rises quietly against the building, its simple, powerful shape inviting a visitor to pause before entering a place where the world’s conflicts are debated.

Nearby stands St. George Slaying the Dragon, a sculpture presented to the United Nations by the Soviet Union. The familiar image of St. George defeating the dragon takes on a different meaning here, surrounded by the flags and institutions of an organisation created in the aftermath of war.

And then there is Antun Augustinčić’s Peace Monument, the mounted figure holding a sword and an olive branch. The Yugoslav/Croatian sculptor had wanted its silhouette to be visible from the East River, so that the idea of peace could announce itself even before a visitor reached the building.

Further along is Carl Fredrik Reuterswärd’s Non-Violence, the bronze revolver with its barrel tied into a knot, a gift from Luxembourg. Nearby, Evgeniy Vuchetich’s Let Us Beat Swords into Ploughshares shows a man transforming a sword into a tool for cultivating the earth.

Taken together, these sculptures seem to form a kind of preface to the United Nations: the human figure, the struggle against violence, the rejection of weapons and the hope that instruments of destruction can be transformed into instruments of peace.

And then you enter the building, where the symbols continue. On an entrance are the words of the great Persian poet Saadi, reminding us that human beings are parts of one body, created from the same essence — and that when one part suffers, the others cannot remain at peace.

And then, inside the building, you encounter the words of Saadi, the great Persian poet, written on a wall.

His famous lines describe human beings as parts of one body, created from the same essence. When one part suffers, the others cannot remain at peace.

I kept returning to those words during these five days.

Because almost everywhere I looked, I saw the world struggling with the very idea they express.

Iran and the United States were at the centre of intense diplomatic activity. Gaza dominated conversations inside the building and protests outside it. The war in Ukraine continued to draw attention, while India and Pakistan brought their familiar confrontation to the international forum.

The United Nations seemed to contain the whole contradiction of our age: an institution built on the idea that humanity can act together, confronted every day by evidence of how difficult that remains.

Outside the gates, protesters gathered in large numbers as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrived to address the UN General Assembly. Inside, delegations walked out during his speech.

And there I was, moving between the demonstrations, the diplomatic meetings, the press conferences and the Assembly hall, doing what journalists do — watching, listening, asking questions and trying to understand what was happening behind the carefully prepared language of diplomacy.

At one point, I actually bumped into Netanyahu.

It was not a planned interview or a formal meeting. It was simply one of those extraordinary moments possible only at the United Nations, where presidents, prime ministers, diplomats, security officers, journalists and interpreters are constantly crossing one another’s paths.

The security arrangements themselves became part of the story.

During the US president’s stay in New York, security around the United Nations was extraordinarily tight. Motorcades moved through sealed streets, access was restricted and every movement of a major leader seemed choreographed. The arrival of leaders such as the Syrian and Turkish presidents added to the atmosphere.

Then the intensity would ease.

A major leader would leave, the barricades would move, the corridors would become less crowded, and suddenly the United Nations would feel almost ordinary again—until another motorcade arrived.

That rhythm is something a television broadcast cannot quite capture.

At the UN, diplomacy is not only what leaders say from the podium. It is also the waiting, the corridors, the security checks, the hurried whispers, the chance encounters and the small conversations between meetings.

Pakistan’s diplomatic role was another important part of my coverage.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the Assembly as Islamabad continued efforts to facilitate dialogue between Iran and the United States. Shehbaz later said Pezeshkian regarded the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding as fully acceptable to Iran and was prepared to move it forward.

That is the other side of covering the UN.

You see confrontation, but you also see countries trying to create channels through which confrontation might be reduced.

And sometimes the most memorable moments have nothing to do with the major powers.

Only at the United Nations could I find myself in a photograph with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman of Bangladesh, Prime Minister Lord Fakafanua of Tonga and Deputy Prime Minister Mulipola Anarosa Ale Molioo of Samoa.

Three leaders from three very different parts of the world, standing together in New York.

Only at the United Nations.

The photograph captures something that statistics cannot. The General Assembly has 193 member states, each represented with one vote. Yet the world represented inside that building is vastly more complicated than a list of countries and votes.

Every delegation carries its own history. Every leader brings his country’s anxieties. Every journalist arrives carrying questions.

And outside, the protesters carry their anger.

For five days, I walked past the sculptures and statues, past the flags and security barriers, past presidents and prime ministers, past demonstrations and diplomatic receptions.

And each time I saw Saadi’s words on the wall, they seemed to ask the same simple question:

If we really are parts of one body, how can one part suffer while the rest remains at peace?

The United Nations has no easy answer. Perhaps that is why the question is still written on its wall.

And perhaps that is why, after five days of covering the world’s most powerful people, the image I carry with me is not of a speech or a motorcade.

It is of people from Bangladesh, Tonga, Samoa and Pakistan standing together for a photograph.

Only at the United Nations.
